summary: We developed an autonomous, comprehensive health monitoring system for astronauts on long-duration space missions, built on four integrated pillars: a smart biosensor patch placed on the thigh (which non-invasively measures bone calcium, 3-Methylhistidine for muscle loss, lactate for acute fatigue, and inflammatory cytokines such as IL-6 in interstitial fluid), a sensory wristband for physical vital signs and sleep tracking, an interactive artificial intelligence for psychological support, and central spacecraft software that filters space-induced signal interference and cross-analyzes all data. This solution directly addresses the challenge of communication latency with Earth and the lack of onboard medical specialists, replacing intermittent and invasive procedures (such as finger-pricks or blood draws) with continuous, ergonomic, and automated monitoring that generates early warnings and personalized countermeasures. It is critical because it proactively safeguards both the physical health and mental well-being of the crew against the accelerated physiological deterioration caused by microgravity, cosmic radiation, and isolation, ensuring crew safety and mission success for future deep-space exploration.
details: The Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts project, developed by the Grupo Tec. Lunático team, consists of an autonomous, continuous, and non-invasive physical and psychological health monitoring system for long-duration space missions, designed to overcome communication latencies with Earth and the absence of onboard medical personnel. The system works by integrating a smart aptamer patch on the thigh to measure biomarkers such as bone calcium, 3-methylhistidine, lactate, and inflammatory cytokines without using needles, protected against cellular clogging via zwitterionic polymers and nitric oxide release; a sensory wristband that records vital signs and sleep; and a central artificial intelligence that wirelessly processes data, filters space interference, and provides conversational psychological support. Its main benefits lie in the early detection of physiological imbalances and the elimination of blood draws, generating a key impact by protecting astronauts from deterioration caused by microgravity, radiation, and isolation, and laying the groundwork for medical autonomy on missions to the Moon, Mars, and beyond. Developed using electrochemical biosensors, microcontrollers, and Python software with SQLite databases and AI tools (Grok, Gemini, Claude), the project stands out for its creativity in multiplexing biochemical assays on a flexible patch and proposing a HUD interface integrated into the helmet visor during extravehicular activities, considering critical factors such as the cryptographic privacy of psychological records, energy self-sufficiency, and adaptation to the hostile conditions of space.
